lead: Some circuits have many storage elements, and solving each differential equation separately gets messy. State-variable analysis collects the inductor currents and capacitor voltages into one vector x. The circuit then becomes two matrix equations, ẋ = Ax + Bu and y = Cx + Du. The eigenvalues of A are the natural frequencies, so you know whether the circuit rings without solving anything. Only a few universities teach this chapter. Circuit simulators and control engineers use it daily.
prereq: You need: 5.4 for the RLC characteristic equation, 5.8 for poles, and basic matrix algebra.

blocks.text: State variables are the quantities that cannot jump when a switch moves: inductor currents iL and capacitor voltages vC (see 5.1). Stack them as x₁, x₂, …, into the state vector x. A circuit with n storage elements has n states.
The circuit becomes two matrix equations:

blocks.where: x is the n × 1 state vector; u holds the m source values; A is n × n; B is n × m.
y holds p outputs; C is p × n; D is p × m; D is the direct feedthrough through resistors.

items: Label each i<sub>L</sub> and v<sub>C</sub> as a state.
Write KVL around inductor loops and KCL at capacitor nodes.
Divide until each derivative stands alone.
Collect coefficients into A and B.
Write each output as a sum of states and sources to read C and D.

blocks.text: The eigenvalues of A are the natural frequencies. Solve:

blocks.where: I is the identity matrix; s is the complex frequency; the roots are the natural frequencies.

blocks.text: This is the same characteristic polynomial as in 5.4. The roots are the poles, so you know whether the circuit rings without solving the differential equation. Real negative roots decay. A pair −σ ± jωd rings at ωd rad/s while decaying. A passive RLC never gives a positive real part. For a 2 × 2 A, compare det(sI − A) with s² + 2ζωns + ωn² to read ωn and ζ.

The figure shows the same algebra. The source u enters through B and adds to the feedback Ax. The integrator turns ẋ into x, so x cannot jump. The output y is read through C. Every circuit simulator builds this loop.

figure.caption: The source enters through B, adds to the feedback Ax, and is integrated to give the state of inductor currents and capacitor voltages. The output is taken through C.

spec.title: State equations as a block diagram
spec.aria: Inputs enter through matrix B, add to the fed-back state through A, pass through integrators to give the state vector, and reach the output through C.

examples.question: A series RLC circuit has R = 1 Ω, L = 1 H, C = 1 F. The input is v<sub>s</sub>(t), and the output is v<sub>C</sub>(t). Take x₁ = i<sub>L</sub> and x₂ = v<sub>C</sub>. Find A, B, C, D and the natural frequencies.
steps: KVL: v<sub>s</sub> = R i<sub>L</sub> + L di<sub>L</sub>/dt + v<sub>C</sub>.
With R = L = C = 1: di<sub>L</sub>/dt = −i<sub>L</sub> − v<sub>C</sub> + v<sub>s</sub>.
KCL at the capacitor: C dv<sub>C</sub>/dt = i<sub>L</sub>, so dv<sub>C</sub>/dt = i<sub>L</sub>.
examples.answer: A = [[−1, −1], [1, 0]], B = [[1], [0]], C = [0 1], D = [0], and the natural frequencies are s = −0.5 ± j0.866 s⁻¹ (ω<sub>n</sub> = 1 rad/s, ζ = 0.5).
examples.check:
import cmath
R, L, C = 1.0, 1.0, 1.0
a = R / L
b = 1.0 / (L * C)
root = cmath.sqrt(a*a - 4*b)
s1 = (-a + root) / 2
print(s1.real)
print(abs(s1.imag))
wn = cmath.sqrt(b).real
print(wn)
print(a / (2 * wn))

traps: Making a resistor voltage or capacitor current a state. Only i<sub>L</sub> and v<sub>C</sub> store energy and stay continuous.
Sign slip in A: the series-RLC i<sub>L</sub> row has −R/L on the diagonal and −1/L against v<sub>C</sub>.
Writing 1/L as 1 in B. A voltage source enters the inductor equation divided by L.
Setting D = 0 for every output. A resistor or inductor voltage usually has a direct path from the source, so D ≠ 0.

quiz.q: Which quantities are the state variables of an RLC circuit?
Why can a resistor voltage not be a state variable?
quiz.a: It can jump at switching and stores no energy.

quiz.q: Series RL: R = 2 Ω, L = 0.5 H, state x = i, input v<sub>s</sub>. Find A and B.

quiz.a: det(sI − A) = s² + 3s + 2 = (s+1)(s+2), so s = −1 and −2 s⁻¹; overdamped.

quiz.q: Series RLC with R = 2 Ω, L = 0.5 H, C = 0.25 F, output v<sub>C</sub>. Write A, B, C, D.
Eigenvalues of A are −0.5 ± j3 s⁻¹. Describe the response.
quiz.a: Decaying oscillation: e<sup>−0.5t</sup> times a sine at 3 rad/s.

beyond: Not for the exam. State-space matrices A, B, C, D are the standard language of control engineering; search state-space representation and controllability and observability. Circuit simulators assemble the same matrices internally, which is why SPICE handles thousands of nodes. Power-electronics engineers average the equations over a switching cycle, called state-space averaging. A later course solves ẋ = Ax + Bu with the state-transition matrix eAt.
